  "title": "KinoTreeDiffuse: Compositional Humanoid Trajectory Amplification via URDF-Factored Iterative Conditional Diffusion",
  "core_problem": "Generating diverse, physically plausible whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation demonstrations by compositionally mixing locomotion and manipulation behaviors remains unsolved in robot joint-space. DreamControl-v2 (arXiv 2604.00202, March 2026) validates that diffusion-generated reference trajectories can train robust RL policies for G1 humanoid skills (91-100% success across 8 tasks), but relies on monolithic text-conditioned generation — the diversity of downstream trajectories is bounded by the training data distribution, with no mechanism for combinatorial composition of locomotion and manipulation behaviors. Human-motion compositional methods (FrankenMotion, MixerMDM, Motion-Adapter) decompose by semantic body groups but operate in SMPL space without physics validation or downstream robot policy evaluation. MixerMDM (CVPR 2025) learns to compose frozen diffusion models at the body-joint level via spatial mixing weights, but operates in human motion space, uses simultaneous blending of frozen models (not conditioned generation), and does not evaluate downstream RL performance. MaskedMimic (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) and MaskedManipulator (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025) pioneer random body-part masking for physics-based character control via RL + distillation, but use C-VAE/RL architectures (not diffusion), train from scratch (not fine-tuning pre-trained models), and produce real-time controllers rather than trajectory datasets for downstream RL. Robot-side generators like Kimodo (NVIDIA, March 2026) produce high-quality G1 motions from text and support kinematic constraint conditioning, but its constraint system was trained exclusively with end-effector and keyframe patterns — body-part-level masks are out-of-distribution. Can we exploit Kimodo's imputation-based constraint mechanism — which shares the mathematical structure of RePaint's mask-agnostic inpainting (x̃_t = m ⊙ x_gt + (1-m) ⊙ x_t) — with URDF-guided body-part factorization and optional LoRA adaptation, to enable compositional loco-manipulation trajectory generation that achieves greater diversity and downstream RL policy quality than monolithic text-conditioned generation?",
  "opportunity": "A key insight is that Kimodo's imputation-based constraint mechanism is mathematically equivalent to RePaint-style inpainting: at each denoising step, constrained joints are replaced with (noised) target values while unconstrained joints are generated freely. RePaint (CVPR 2022) demonstrated that this imputation mechanism generalizes to arbitrary mask patterns — including those never seen during training — because it operates at the level of individual denoising steps rather than requiring mask-pattern-specific learned representations. However, a critical caveat applies: Kimodo's Phase 2 training uses specific constraint patterns (full-body keyframes, random subsets of hands/feet positions/rotations, 2D root position/heading, foot contact configurations), and body-part-level masking (e.g., 'fix all lower-body joints while generating upper-body') was NEVER in its training distribution. Whether the RePaint generalization principle extends to Kimodo's motion-specific architecture with dual classifier-free guidance (w_text=2, w_constr=2) is an empirical question that forms the central hypothesis of this work. MDM (ICLR 2023) provides supporting evidence: it demonstrated spatial body-part inpainting in human motion diffusion using the same imputation mechanism, though in SMPL space rather than robot joint-space. DreamControl-v2 provides complementary validation: its pipeline (train diffusion in robot space → generate diverse trajectories → train RL policies) achieves strong results on G1, confirming that the overall paradigm works — what remains is whether compositional body-part generation can improve trajectory diversity and downstream policy quality beyond monolithic text conditioning.

Kimodo's G1-SEED-v1 checkpoint (282M parameters, trained on 288h BONES-SEED data) and its complete training hyperparameters are publicly documented: T=1000 diffusion steps, Adam-atan2 optimizer at lr=2e-5, Smooth L1 loss with per-component weights, EMA every 10 steps with decay 0.995, 6D rotation representation, and a two-stage transformer denoiser (16 layers, 8 heads, dim 1024). Kimodo's public repository provides ONLY inference code — no training scripts, data loaders, or fine-tuning infrastructure. The zero-shot iterative conditional generation pipeline requires only Kimodo's inference API with its imputation mechanism. For the LoRA secondary contribution, we implement fine-tuning from the inference codebase using documented hyperparameters. All infrastructure exists: (1) Kimodo G1-SEED-v1 provides the backbone; (2) BONES-SEED provides 288h of G1-retargeted motions with up to 6 NL descriptions per motion plus temporal segmentation; (3) OmniRetarget provides 4.0h of publicly available G1 loco-manipulation trajectories (3.0h robot-object + 0.5h robot-terrain + 0.5h robot-object-terrain); (4) ProtoMotions provides GPU-accelerated kinematic-to-dynamic conversion; (5) SkillBench provides 8 G1 loco-manipulation tasks with evaluation metrics.",
  "landscape": "**Diffusion→trajectories→RL pipeline for G1 (direct paradigm validation):** DreamControl-v2 (arXiv 2604.00202, March 2026) is the most directly relevant prior work — it trains a guided diffusion model directly in G1's motion space using retargeted human motion data (AMASS, GRAB, Nymeria, OmniRetarget; 29.6K samples), generates reference trajectories conditioned on text and spatio-temporal controls, and trains downstream RL policies achieving 91-100% success across 8 tasks on real G1 hardware. Critically, DreamControl-v2 uses monolithic text-conditioned generation with no body-part compositional mechanism — trajectory diversity is bounded by training data. Our work extends this validated paradigm with compositional body-part generation: URDF-factored iterative conditioning enables N_loco × N_manip diverse trajectories from a single pre-trained model, targeting the diversity bottleneck that DreamControl-v2 does not address. DreamControl-v1 (arXiv 2509.14353) used an off-the-shelf human-space diffusion model with IK, requiring manual trajectory filtering; v2's robot-space training eliminates this, paralleling our use of Kimodo's robot-space model.

**Body-part compositional motion diffusion (human motion space):** MixerMDM (CVPR 2025, arXiv 2504.01019) is the closest prior art for body-part composition — it learns spatial mixing weights (per-joint, per-timestep) to blend denoising outputs of two frozen pre-trained motion diffusion models. Key differences: MixerMDM composes *frozen* models via simultaneous weighted blending, operates in SMPL/HumanML3D space, and evaluates motion quality metrics (FID, alignment) rather than downstream RL policy performance. FrankenMotion (arXiv 2601.10909, Jan 2026) trains a diffusion model with part-level temporally-structured text prompts in SMPL space — critically, they found that naive body-part composition produces 'unsmooth transitions,' motivating purpose-built part-level training. Motion-Adapter (arXiv 2604.16135, April 2026) addresses compound action synthesis via attention-mask-guided denoising. CompDiffuser (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight, arXiv 2503.05153) achieves compositional trajectory stitching through temporal overlap and bidirectional diffusion — a temporal analog to our spatial body-part approach. EnergyMoGen (CVPR 2025) and DeMoGen (arXiv 2512.22324, Dec 2025) compose motions via energy-based diffusion. All operate in human motion space without physics validation or robot RL evaluation.

**Physics-based masked motion controllers (NVIDIA):** MaskedMimic (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024, arXiv 2409.14393) formulates physics-based character control as motion inpainting via random body-part masking. MaskedManipulator (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025, arXiv 2505.19086) extends MaskedMimic to whole-body loco-manipulation. Both use C-VAE/RL architectures (not diffusion), train from scratch via RL+distillation, and produce real-time controllers rather than trajectory datasets. Our work brings MaskedMimic's masking insight into the diffusion paradigm on a pre-trained robot-specific model.

**Diffusion-based humanoid control with inpainting:** BeyondMimic (arXiv 2508.08241, UC Berkeley) proposes a unified latent diffusion model for humanoid control that supports motion inpainting, skill composition, and dynamic behavior switching via classifier guidance, with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. While it targets real-time control rather than trajectory dataset generation for downstream RL, its diffusion-based inpainting and composition approach validates that diffusion models can generalize to novel conditioning patterns at inference time.

**Robot motion diffusion (G1-specific):** Kimodo (NVIDIA, arXiv 2603.15546, March 2026) is a 282M-parameter two-stage transformer denoiser trained on 288h BONES-SEED (SEED variant), generating G1 motions from text in 2-5s. Its constraint conditioning uses binary masking with imputation and dual classifier-free guidance. Phase 2 training uses specific constraint patterns: full-body keyframes, random subsets of hands/feet positions/rotations, 2D root position/heading, foot contact configurations. Body-part-level masks are NOT in its training distribution — our use of body-part masking is OOD and constitutes an empirical hypothesis. MotionBricks (NVIDIA, arXiv 2604.24833, April 2026) provides real-time latent generative motion for G1 with training code, but uses VQVAE + latent backbone (not diffusion). REFINE-DP (arXiv 2603.13707, March 2026) demonstrates diffusion policy fine-tuning via RL for humanoid loco-manipulation but does not address compositional generation. Psi0 (arXiv 2603.12263, March 2026) is a VLA foundation model using flow-based action prediction.

**Mask-agnostic diffusion inpainting:** RePaint (CVPR 2022, arXiv 2201.09865) demonstrated that pre-trained DDPMs can perform inpainting with arbitrary binary masks — including patterns never seen during training — by replacing masked regions with noised target values at each denoising step. Its resampling trick (re-noising and re-denoising at mask boundaries) improves coherence at the cost of additional denoising steps. We adopt this principle for body-part conditioning: Kimodo's imputation mechanism (x̃_t = m ⊙ x_gt + (1-m) ⊙ x_t) is structurally identical to RePaint's approach. Whether this generalizes from image DDPMs to motion-specific transformers with dual CFG is our central empirical question.

**Compositional diffusion theory:** Reduce Reuse Recycle (Du et al., ICML 2023) identifies bias in naive score composition and proposes MCMC correction. Mechanisms of Projective Composition (Bradley et al., ICML 2025) proves score composition requires approximate factorization. Refining Compositional Diffusion (arXiv 2605.03075, May 2026) documents mode-averaging. These works motivate our iterative conditional generation (sequential complete diffusion processes) over alternating score composition.

**LoRA fine-tuning for diffusion models:** LoRA (Hu et al., ICLR 2022) is standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of diffusion transformers. We apply LoRA to Kimodo's attention layers for the first time.

**Data generation for humanoid RL:** OmniRetarget (arXiv 2509.26633) provides 4.0h of publicly available G1 loco-manipulation trajectories. ProtoMotions provides GPU-accelerated physics tracking for G1.

No existing work uses a pre-trained robot motion diffusion model's imputation mechanism for systematic body-part compositional trajectory generation — testing OOD mask generalization with optional LoRA enhancement — with physics projection and downstream RL evaluation. DreamControl-v2 validates the pipeline paradigm; we extend it with compositional generation.",
  "approach": "We propose KinoTreeDiffuse, a framework testing whether Kimodo's imputation-based constraint conditioning generalizes to URDF-guided body-part masks for compositional loco-manipulation trajectory generation — an OOD application of RePaint-style inpainting principles to robot motion diffusion. The framework has two tiers: a zero-shot pipeline (primary contribution) that requires only Kimodo's inference API, and LoRA-enhanced generation (secondary contribution) that improves conditional quality via lightweight fine-tuning.

**0. Preliminary Diversity Analysis (Day 1-2).** Before the main pipeline, we establish the empirical case for compositional generation over monolithic text prompting. We generate 50 compound text-prompted motions from Kimodo (e.g., 'walk toward the shelf while raising your right hand,' 'jog forward while waving both arms') and measure their diversity in joint-angle space (mean pairwise distance, coverage of joint-angle manifold). We then generate 50 compositionally generated motions (5 locomotion prompts × 10 manipulation prompts) using the zero-shot pipeline. We hypothesize that compositional diversity will be measurably higher for two reasons: (a) compound text prompts are underrepresented in BONES-SEED's training data compared to atomic descriptions, limiting the model's coverage of the compound motion manifold; (b) the combinatorial product of independently sampled locomotion and manipulation components explores regions of joint-angle space inaccessible to monolithic text conditioning. If this preliminary analysis shows no diversity advantage, it signals a fundamental limitation and we pivot to analyzing when/why compositional generation fails — itself a valuable contribution.

**1. URDF-Guided Body-Part Factorization.** We parse the G1 URDF to define two kinematic subtrees: a lower-body group (root/pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, feet — locomotion, including boundary joints at the lower torso) and an upper-body group (torso, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hands — manipulation). This determines which of the 34 G1 joints are constrained vs. generated in each phase. The factorization is encoded as binary masks compatible with Kimodo's imputation format.

**2. Iterative Conditional Generation with RePaint-Style Imputation (Primary Contribution).** We frame body-part conditioning as RePaint-style inpainting applied to Kimodo's inference pipeline. Instead of composing scores within the denoising loop — which suffers from mode-averaging (RCD, 2026), factorization violations (Bradley et al., ICML 2025), and unsmooth transitions (FrankenMotion, 2026) — we run sequential complete diffusion processes:

  Phase 1 (Locomotion): Generate lower-body trajectory via Kimodo's full denoising (T=1000 steps) with locomotion text prompt and upper-body unconstrained.

  Phase 2 (Manipulation): Generate upper-body trajectory via a second complete denoising with manipulation text prompt and lower-body joints fixed as constraints using Kimodo's imputation mechanism (x̃_t = m ⊙ x_lower + (1-m) ⊙ x_t, with w_constr=2). This is OOD with respect to Kimodo's training constraint patterns (which used end-effector/keyframe constraints, not body-part masks). We explicitly test whether the imputation mechanism generalizes following the RePaint principle: because imputation operates at each individual denoising step — replacing constrained values before each denoiser forward pass — it does not require the mask pattern itself to have been learned.

  Phase 2b (RePaint Resampling Variant): Following RePaint's resampling trick, we optionally add r=5-10 noise-denoise cycles at each denoising step near the body-part boundary (lower torso/pelvis joints), improving coherence between independently generated body parts. This costs r× more denoising steps at boundary joints but is trivial to implement with Kimodo's inference API.

  Phase 3 (Optional Refinement): Re-generate lower-body conditioned on upper-body output. 1-2 iterations suffice.

Diversity is achieved by sampling different locomotion × manipulation combinations — the combinatorial product yields exponentially more compositions than exist in training data. The zero-shot pipeline requires NO modifications to Kimodo's code — only its public inference API with constraint inputs.

**3. LoRA-Based Masked Fine-Tuning (Secondary Contribution).** While the zero-shot pipeline tests OOD generalization, LoRA fine-tuning can bring body-part conditioning into the training distribution, improving conditional quality. We implement a training loop from Kimodo's inference codebase — realistic scope is 500-800 lines of non-trivial PyTorch code covering:

  (a) Data loading: BONES-SEED format parsing (motion representation with 6D rotations, smoothed root, temporal annotations) and OmniRetarget integration.
  (b) LoRA injection: Rank-16 adapters into query/key/value projections of 16 transformer layers (~8M trainable parameters, ~3% of 282M total).
  (c) Masked denoising objective: With probability p_mask=0.5, replace either upper-body or lower-body joint channels with Gaussian noise while preserving the other part's clean signal, computing loss only on masked joints. This directly trains the conditional distributions p(upper|lower,text_manip) and p(lower|upper,text_loco).
  (d) Body-part text annotations: BONES-SEED includes up to 6 NL descriptions per motion plus temporal segmentation with precise timestamps. We derive body-part-specific labels via: (i) parsing existing descriptions for body-part keywords ('walking' → lower, 'reaching' → upper); (ii) supplementing with per-body-part joint velocity statistics via LLM prompting for ambiguous cases; (iii) manually verifying 100 random annotations against motion visualizations.
  (e) Optimizer and training: Adam-atan2, lr=2e-5, Smooth L1 loss with published per-component weights, EMA decay 0.995. Training on BONES-SEED (288h, 142K motions) + OmniRetarget (4.0h).

  No physics training losses: Physics consistency is handled entirely by post-generation projection.

  Budget: 4-6 days for implementation, ~8-12h on 1×A100 for training.

**4. Post-Composition Physics Projection.** After iterative conditional generation, a lightweight quadratic program (~0.1s per trajectory) optimizes for: (a) centroidal dynamics consistency between upper and lower body; (b) CoM within support polygon; (c) G1 joint torque limits from URDF. Trajectories failing projection (>5% of joints exceeding limits) are rejected and re-sampled.

**5. Kinematic-to-Dynamic Pipeline.** Projected trajectories are converted to physics-validated RL demonstrations via ProtoMotions' GPU-accelerated tracking. Tracking success rate serves as a physics quality metric.

**6. Evaluation on SkillBench (3 Tasks).** We evaluate on 3 SkillBench G1 tasks spanning difficulty levels: FarReach (Easy), BoxPush (Medium), PackageCarry (Hard). Baselines:
  (1) **DreamControl-v2** — the primary paradigm baseline: diffusion→trajectories→RL with monolithic text conditioning (no body-part composition). We use their published results or reproduce using their pipeline.
  (2) **Kimodo text-prompted** — compound text prompts (e.g., 'walk forward while reaching'). Tests whether Kimodo's LLM2Vec text encoding already handles compound prompts well enough.
  (3) **Zero-shot iterative conditioning (no resampling)** — our pipeline without RePaint resampling or LoRA; isolates the value of basic imputation-based body-part factorization.
  (4) **Zero-shot + RePaint resampling** — adds noise-denoise cycles at body-part boundaries; tests whether resampling improves coherence.
  (5) **LoRA-enhanced iterative generation** — our full pipeline; isolates the value of LoRA fine-tuning.
  (6) **OmniRetarget** — optimization-based G1 trajectories (4.0h available).
  (7) **Naive concatenation** — lower-body from one sample + upper-body from another, no conditioning (ablation).

  Key metrics: downstream RL policy success rate (primary), trajectory diversity (mean pairwise distance in joint-angle space), physics violation rate (ProtoMotions tracking failure rate), and data efficiency curve.

**Early Checkpoint (Day 8-10).** Before committing to full SkillBench evaluation, we evaluate: (a) zero-shot imputation quality — does Kimodo produce coherent motions with body-part masks? If coherence is poor (<30% tracking success), the OOD hypothesis is rejected and we focus the paper on the LoRA approach; (b) zero-shot vs. RePaint-resampled vs. LoRA-tuned conditional generation quality using FID and diversity metrics on held-out BONES-SEED motions. This checkpoint determines which variants to carry forward to full RL evaluation.

**Possible Outcomes and Their Contributions:**
  (a) Zero-shot works well → demonstrates that RePaint-style imputation generalizes to robot motion diffusion, enabling training-free compositional generation.
  (b) Zero-shot fails, LoRA succeeds → demonstrates that body-part conditioning requires explicit training but can be achieved efficiently via LoRA.
  (c) Both improve diversity but not RL performance → reveals that trajectory diversity alone is insufficient for downstream policy quality, an important negative result.
  (d) Compositional generation underperforms text-prompted → establishes empirical limits of factored generation, also valuable.

**Key Differentiation.** From DreamControl-v2: compositional body-part generation enabling combinatorial diversity vs. monolithic text conditioning; uses pre-trained Kimodo (not custom-trained diffusion); tests OOD constraint generalization. From MixerMDM: robot-specific model, LoRA fine-tuning, iterative conditional generation, downstream RL evaluation. From MaskedMimic: diffusion not C-VAE/RL, LoRA fine-tune pre-trained model, trajectory datasets not real-time controllers. From BeyondMimic: trajectory dataset generation for downstream RL amplification vs. real-time latent diffusion control; URDF-structured body-part factorization vs. classifier-guided composition.",

  "description": "We address compositional generation of diverse, physically plausible humanoid loco-manipulation demonstrations by testing whether a pre-trained robot motion diffusion model's imputation-based constraint conditioning generalizes to URDF-guided body-part masks — an out-of-distribution application that we frame as RePaint-style inpainting in robot motion space. We introduce a two-tier framework: (1) a zero-shot iterative conditional generation pipeline (primary contribution) that uses URDF-guided body-part factorization to decompose G1's 34 joints into locomotion and manipulation subtrees, then runs sequential complete diffusion processes — first generating lower-body locomotion, then upper-body manipulation conditioned on fixed lower-body constraints via Kimodo's imputation — with an optional RePaint resampling variant (noise-denoise cycles at body-part boundaries for improved coherence), followed by post-composition physics projection via quadratic programming; (2) LoRA-based masked fine-tuning (secondary contribution, 500-800 lines of implementation, 4-6 days) that injects rank-16 adapters (~8M trainable parameters) into Kimodo's transformer attention layers with a masked denoising objective inspired by MaskedMimic, explicitly training the conditional distributions p(upper|lower,text) and p(lower|upper,text) to bring body-part conditioning into the training distribution. The framework has two tiers: a zero-shot pipeline (primary contribution) that requires only Kimodo's inference API, and LoRA-enhanced generation (secondary contribution) that improves conditional quality via lightweight fine-tuning.

**0. Preliminary Diversity Analysis (Day 1-2).** Before the main pipeline, we establish the empirical case for compositional generation over monolithic text prompting. We generate 50 compound text-prompted motions from Kimodo (e.g., 'walk toward the shelf while raising your right hand,' 'jog forward while waving both arms') and measure their diversity in joint-angle space (mean pairwise distance, coverage of joint-angle manifold). We then generate 50 compositionally generated motions (5 locomotion prompts × 10 manipulation prompts) using the zero-shot pipeline. We hypothesize that compositional diversity will be measurably higher for two reasons: (a) compound text prompts are underrepresented in BONES-SEED's training data compared to atomic descriptions, limiting the model's coverage of the compound motion manifold; (b) the combinatorial product of independently sampled locomotion and manipulation components explores regions of joint-angle space inaccessible to monolithic text conditioning. If this preliminary analysis shows no diversity advantage, it signals a fundamental limitation and we pivot to analyzing when/why compositional generation fails — itself a valuable contribution.

**1. URDF-Guided Body-Part Factorization.** We parse the G1 URDF to define two kinematic subtrees: a lower-body group (root/pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, feet — locomotion, including boundary joints at the lower torso) and an upper-body group (torso, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hands — manipulation). This determines which of the 34 G1 joints are constrained vs. generated in each phase. The factorization is encoded as binary masks compatible with Kimodo's imputation format.

**2. Iterative Conditional Generation with RePaint-Style Imputation (Primary Contribution).** We frame body-part conditioning as RePaint-style inpainting applied to Kimodo's inference pipeline. Instead of composing scores within the denoising loop — which suffers from mode-averaging (RCD, 2026), factorization violations (Bradley et al., ICML 2025), and unsmooth transitions (FrankenMotion, 2026) — we run sequential complete diffusion processes:

  Phase 1 (Locomotion): Generate lower-body trajectory via Kimodo's full denoising (T=1000 steps) with locomotion text prompt and upper-body unconstrained.

  Phase 2 (Manipulation): Generate upper-body trajectory via a second complete denoising with manipulation text prompt and lower-body joints fixed as constraints using Kimodo's imputation mechanism (x̃_t = m ⊙ x_lower + (1-m) ⊙ x_t, with w_constr=2). This is OOD with respect to Kimodo's training constraint patterns (which used end-effector/keyframe constraints, not body-part masks). We explicitly test whether the imputation mechanism generalizes following the RePaint principle: because imputation operates at each individual denoising step — replacing constrained values before each denoiser forward pass — it does not require the mask pattern itself to have been learned.

  Phase 2b (RePaint Resampling Variant): Following RePaint's resampling trick, we optionally add r=5-10 noise-denoise cycles at each denoising step near the body-part boundary (lower torso/pelvis joints), improving coherence between independently generated body parts. This costs r× more denoising steps at boundary joints but is trivial to implement with Kimodo's inference API.

  Phase 3 (Optional Refinement): Re-generate lower-body conditioned on upper-body output. 1-2 iterations suffice.

Diversity is achieved by sampling different locomotion × manipulation combinations — the combinatorial product yields exponentially more compositions than exist in training data. The zero-shot pipeline requires NO modifications to Kimodo's code — only its public inference API with constraint inputs.

**3. LoRA-Based Masked Fine-Tuning (Secondary Contribution).** While the zero-shot pipeline tests OOD generalization, LoRA fine-tuning can bring body-part conditioning into the training distribution, improving conditional quality. We implement a training loop from Kimodo's inference codebase — realistic scope is 500-800 lines of non-trivial PyTorch code covering:

  (a) Data loading: BONES-SEED format parsing (motion representation with 6D rotations, smoothed root, temporal annotations) and OmniRetarget integration.
  (b) LoRA injection: Rank-16 adapters into query/key/value projections of 16 transformer layers (~8M trainable parameters, ~3% of 282M total).
  (c) Masked denoising objective: With probability p_mask=0.5, replace either upper-body or lower-body joint channels with Gaussian noise while preserving the other part's clean signal, computing loss only on masked joints. This directly trains the conditional distributions p(upper|lower,text_manip) and p(lower|upper,text_loco).
  (d) Body-part text annotations: BONES-SEED includes up to 6 NL descriptions per motion plus temporal segmentation with precise timestamps. We derive body-part-specific labels via: (i) parsing existing descriptions for body-part keywords ('walking' → lower, 'reaching' → upper); (ii) supplementing with per-body-part joint velocity statistics via LLM prompting for ambiguous cases; (iii) manually verifying 100 random annotations against motion visualizations.
  (e) Optimizer and training: Adam-atan2, lr=2e-5, Smooth L1 loss with published per-component weights, EMA decay 0.995. Training on BONES-SEED (288h, 142K motions) + OmniRetarget (4.0h).

  No physics training losses: Physics consistency is handled entirely by post-generation projection.

  Budget: 4-6 days for implementation, ~8-12h on 1×A100 for training.

**4. Post-Composition Physics Projection.** After iterative conditional generation, a lightweight quadratic program (~0.1s per trajectory) optimizes for: (a) centroidal dynamics consistency between upper and lower body; (b) CoM within support polygon; (c) G1 joint torque limits from URDF. Trajectories failing projection (>5% of joints exceeding limits) are rejected and re-sampled.

**5. Kinematic-to-Dynamic Pipeline.** Projected trajectories are converted to physics-validated RL demonstrations via ProtoMotions' GPU-accelerated tracking. Tracking success rate serves as a physics quality metric.

**6. Evaluation on SkillBench (3 Tasks).** We evaluate on 3 SkillBench G1 tasks spanning difficulty levels: FarReach (Easy), BoxPush (Medium), PackageCarry (Hard). Baselines:
  (1) **DreamControl-v2** — the primary paradigm baseline: diffusion→trajectories→RL with monolithic text conditioning (no body-part composition). We use their published results or reproduce using their pipeline.
  (2) **Kimodo text-prompted** — compound text prompts (e.g., 'walk forward while reaching'). Tests whether Kimodo's LLM2Vec text encoding already handles compound prompts well enough.
  (3) **Zero-shot iterative conditioning (no resampling)** — our pipeline without RePaint resampling or LoRA; isolates the value of basic imputation-based body-part factorization.
  (4) **Zero-shot + RePaint resampling** — adds noise-denoise cycles at body-part boundaries; tests whether resampling improves coherence.
  (5) **LoRA-enhanced iterative generation** — our full pipeline; isolates the value of LoRA fine-tuning.
  (6) **OmniRetarget** — optimization-based G1 trajectories (4.0h available).
  (7) **Naive concatenation** — lower-body from one sample + upper-body from another, no conditioning (ablation).

  Key metrics: downstream RL policy success rate (primary), trajectory diversity (mean pairwise distance in joint-angle space), physics violation rate (ProtoMotions tracking failure rate), and data efficiency curve.

**Early Checkpoint (Day 8-10).** Before committing to full SkillBench evaluation, we evaluate: (a) zero-shot imputation quality — does Kimodo produce coherent motions with body-part masks? If coherence is poor (<30% tracking success), the OOD hypothesis is rejected and we focus the paper on the LoRA approach; (b) zero-shot vs. RePaint-resampled vs. LoRA-tuned conditional generation quality using FID and diversity metrics on held-out BONES-SEED motions. This checkpoint determines which variants to carry forward to full RL evaluation.

**Possible Outcomes and Their Contributions:**
  (a) Zero-shot works well → demonstrates that RePaint-style imputation generalizes to robot motion diffusion, enabling training-free compositional generation.
  (b) Zero-shot fails, LoRA succeeds → demonstrates that body-part conditioning requires explicit training but can be achieved efficiently via LoRA.
  (c) Both improve diversity but not RL performance → reveals that trajectory diversity alone is insufficient for downstream policy quality, an important negative result.
  (d) Compositional generation underperforms text-prompted → establishes empirical limits of factored generation, also valuable.

**Key Differentiation.** From DreamControl-v2: compositional body-part generation enabling combinatorial diversity vs. monolithic text conditioning; uses pre-trained Kimodo (not custom-trained diffusion); tests OOD constraint generalization. ## What Guidance Does in Masked Discrete Diffusion

When the full data distribution is a mixture over classes and the goal is to sample from a specific class, guidance amplifies class-specific regions while suppresses regions shared with other classes. By deriving an explicit solution to the guided reverse dynamics, the way guidance influences sampling behavior can be precisely characterized.

## Guidance Failure Modes

The research has identified several important failure modes of guidance in masked discrete diffusion:

**Early-Stage Guidance Problems:** High guidance early in sampling (when inputs are heavily masked) harms generation quality, while late-stage guidance improves it.

**Unmasking Rate Issues:** Current CFG implementations can unintentionally cause imbalanced transitions, such as unmasking too rapidly during the early stages of generation, which degrades the quality of the resulting samples.

**Limited Amenability of Masked Diffusion:** Masked diffusion models are less amenable to guidance, since once a token is unmasked at some time t it remains so for all subsequent steps. In contrast, with uniform noising, intermediate latents can be refined multiple times throughout the denoising process.

These findings highlight that guidance effectiveness in masked discrete diffusion depends critically on the timing and implementation, with early guidance particularly problematic due to rapid unmasking rates that destabilize the generation process.

The problems with classifier-free guidance actually stem from the off-manifold phenomenon associated with CFG, rather than the diffusion models themselves. Off-manifold phenomenon of CFG arise from: (a) the typical CFG scale ω > 1.0 which leads to extrapolation and deviation from the piecewise linear data manifold, and (b) CFG's renoising process, which introduces a nonzero offset from the correct manifold.

**CFG++ Solution:**

CFG++ tackles the off-manifold challenges inherent in traditional CFG by reformulating text-guidance as an inverse problem with a text-conditioned score matching loss. - EP-CFG rescales guided predictions to preserve the energy (norm) of the conditional prediction, reducing contrast and over-saturation artifacts.

## Kimodo: Constraint Guidance and Imputation Mechanism

Kimodo is a kinematic motion diffusion model that trains at scale to enable intuitive authoring of high-quality motions through text prompting and an extensive set of kinematic constraints.

### Constraint Conditioning Approach

The method is most related to approaches that use imputation to condition generation by directly overwriting constraints in the input motion, with CondMDI using the same imputation approach with a concatenated mask as input to the denoiser. At each step of the denoising process, the model takes in an embedding of the text prompt, a set of kinematic constraints, and the current noisy motion. Constraints are specified using the same motion representation as the input motion, and are used to overwrite the corresponding values in the noisy motion. Additionally, a mask indicating which elements are constrained is concatenated to the input motion.

### Dual CFG (Classifier-Free Guidance) for Motion Diffusion

The implementation supports classifier-free guidance with options for no CFG, regular guidance with one weight, or separated guidance with two weights for text vs. constraints.

### Two-Stage Architecture

The two-stage denoiser design is key to maximizing motion quality and control accuracy together. The global root representation used in the first stage enables conditioning on sparse global root constraints through direct imputation, while the second stage benefits from being conditioned on a more invariant local root representation. Unlike prior two-stage approaches, this two-stage model is interleaved since the root and body predictions are made at every denoising step. Prior work performs the root denoising process in full before generating the body motion, while this model enables root and body corrections throughout denoising to attain better alignment in the end.

# Kimodo: Constraint Conditioning Mechanisms

## 1. Dual Classifier-Free Guidance

The guidance mechanism decomposes text and constraint conditioning separately:

**Formula:** `x̂₀ = D∅ + w_text(D_text - D∅) + w_constr(D_constr - D∅)`

Where:
- D∅ = model output with no conditioning
- D_text = output using only text (no constraints)
- D_constr = output using only constraints (no text)
- **Default weights:** w_text = 2, w_constr = 2 (user-adjustable at test time)

This allows independent control over text influence versus constraint influence on generation.

## 2. Constraint Imputation Mechanism

Constraints are applied through direct feature overwriting at each denoising step:

**Formula:** `x̃_t = m ⊙ x_tgt + (1-m) ⊙ x_t`

Where:
- m = binary control mask indicating constrained features
- x_tgt = target pose features (the constraint specification)
- x_t = noisy motion at step t
- ⊙ = element-wise multiplication

The mask concatenates with imputed motion as final input: `x_in = [x̃_t; m]`

## 3. Phase 2 Training Constraint Patterns

During the second 500k training steps, randomly sampled constraint patterns included:

- Full-body joint positions at sparse keyframes
- Random hand/foot position and rotation subsets at sparse keyframes
- 2D root position/heading at sparse keyframes
- Dense 2D root position/heading paths
- Foot contact configurations at sparse keyframes
- Mixed constraint patterns (25% of time)
- No constraints (10% of time)

Maximum keyframes increased linearly from 1 to 20 during phase 2, with sampling biased toward fewer keyframes.

## 4. Out-of-Distribution Constraints

The paper does not explicitly discuss handling out-of-distribution constraints. However, it mentions applying "random perturbations on global translation and heading of constraints" for evaluation generalization, suggesting robustness was tested but specific failure modes aren't addressed.

## 5. Guidance and Constraint Masking Interaction

The separated guidance operates at the denoising step level after constraint imputation. The control mask indicates *which* features are constrained; guidance weights then modulate how strongly text and constraints influence the overall prediction, effectively creating a weighted blend between unconstrained, text-only, and constraint-only outputs at each iteration.

## Overview of Permutation Tests

A permutation test is a statistical significance test that estimates the null distribution of a test statistic by repeatedly permuting data points between groups, with each permutation generating a new sample from this distribution.

## Key Advantages

Permutation tests exist for any test statistic, regardless of whether or not its distribution is known. This makes them particularly flexible. Permutation testing can be applied to any test statistic and makes no assumptions about the underlying distribution being normal.

## Statistical Significance and Power

Permutation-based approaches offer alternative methods to test for significance that relax the assumptions made by parametric tests. Regarding robustness, the permutation versions of the Welch t-test and the Brunner-Munzel test are found to be robust at both α = 0.005 and α = 0.05.

## Sample Size Considerations

An appropriate sample size is still needed - if you only have 3 respondents in each group, any form of hypothesis testing is probably a pointless exercise.

## Permutation Count

For computational implementation, using 100,000 permutations reduces the uncertainty near p = 0.05 to ±0.1% and allows p-values as small as 0.00001.

## Diversity Metrics in PERMANOVA

**Compositional Generation in Diffusion Models:**

Recent research proves an exact equivalence between a specific compositional structure (conditional projective composition) and scores with sparse dependencies on both pixels and conditioners (local conditional scores). ## Overview

CondMDI is a unified and flexible method for motion in-betweening based on a masked conditional diffusion model called Conditional Motion Diffusion In-betweening. CondMDI is a masked conditional diffusion model for motion in-betweening.

## Key Capabilities

CondMDI is capable of generating precise and diverse motions that conform to a flexible range of user-specified spatial constraints, as well as text conditioning, allowing for arbitrary dense-or-sparse keyframe placement and partial keyframe constraints while generating high-quality motions that are diverse and coherent with the given keyframes.

## Technical Approach

To condition the model on keyframes, the approach replaces the noisy input motion with the given keyframes over the provided frames, and concatenates the observation mask to further inform the model of the keyframe locations, with the model trained on randomly sampled keyframes with randomly sampled joints, together with a mask that indicates the observed keyframes and features.

## Application

CondMDI allows for text prompts to be used as an additional condition to control the generated motions. Evaluation is done on the HumanML3D dataset.

## Publication

CondMDI was published at Special Interest Group on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques Conference Conference Papers '24 (SIGGRAPH Conference Papers '24), July 27-August 1, 2024, Denver, CO, USA.
